speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: BEREAVEMENT OF HON. MEMBER FOR WINNIPEG NORTH CENTRE EXPRESSION OF SYMPATHY ON PASSING AWAY OF WIFE OF MR. STANLEY KNOWLES
speechtext:
Order, please. Before calling motions pursuant to Standing Order 43-I will, of course, try to reserve an appropriate length of time for that and extend the question period if necessary-hon. members will have noticed the rather singular absence from the House today of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). This absence from this House is so rare that it is worthy of note on the occasion it does occur. I wish I could say that the hon. member's absence was due to some happy event, but it is not. Hon. members will be saddened to learn that the wife of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre passed away last night and he is, of course, in Winnipeg at this time.
Hon. members of all parties have spoken to me, and rather than having individual comments at this time, particularly in view of the suddenness of the event, perhaps I could speak on behalf of all members of the House in saying to this very distinguished parliamentarian of such long service and great devotion and affection for parliament that all of us wish in some way to reach out to him in this moment of sadness.
Our thoughts and prayers on this day are with him and his family who are all together in Winnipeg. We know the hon. member left earlier this week to be in Winnipeg because of some news and returned to his duties here only too briefly, to be called again last night to be told of this very sad news. I am sure I speak on behalf of all hon. members in saying our prayers and thoughts are with him. I will, of course, be taking the appropriate steps to extend that sentiment directly to Mr. Knowles the moment I leave the chair here today.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT CONSULTS PROVINCES ON AMENDMENTS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to introduce a motion and ask for the unanimous consent of the House under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Considering that the Prime Minister stated yesterday that it is difficult to decide whether it is advisable to unveil the constitutional proposals to the House of Commons or during an election campaign; considering that according to the confeder-ative spirit the provinces should be first to decide, or settle as the Prime Minister said, the future of confederation, although we recognize that the federal government could take part at the unanimous invitation of the provinces, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert):
That the Prime Minister undertake serious consultations with the provinces to know what they want instead of forcing his will on them, thus antagonizing them and giving rise to the present state of confusion instead of creating the harmony suggested by the Social Credit Party.

Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. On March 16, 1978, the Northern Flood Agreement was ratified by the five Indian bands comprising the northern flood committee. However, it will become "another meaningless paper commitment" if the Indian people cannot participate in the actual implementation of the agreement.
In view of the fact the former minister of Indian Affairs, the present Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand), recognized the committee's need for continued funding during the transitional period after the agreement had been ratified, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp):
That the present minister of Indian affairs meet with the northern flood committee and ensure funding be continued throughout implementation stages of the agreement.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I seek the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that several months ago the House adopted a motion calling for a change in our Standing Orders which would allow the public to be present in the galleries and join us in the prayers at the beginning of our daily meetings, a motion which was referred to our Committee on Procedure and Organization for recommendations; and in view also of the fact that the nature and length of our current prayers should be modified to reflect better the new ecumenical spirit, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That the House urge the caucus of each and every political party represented in the House to provide our committee on procedure, within the next two weeks, with the text of a prayer in which all Canadians could join to ask Our Lord and Father for His guidance, with instructions to the committee to report before the end of the current legislature.

From the month of April and on for nine consecutive months, Quebec's Marine Industries will lay off 100 employees each month, bringing the number of workers down from 2,500 to 1,600. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert):
That the House ask the government to take action to stop this drain of 900 workers.

subsubtopic: SALES TAX-GOVERNMENT STUDY OF QUEBEC PROPOSALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Because of the current concern in Quebec about the budgetary proposal and also because of the impending lay-off of 1,900 workers announced by Marine Industries and Northern Telecom, I should like to ask the Minister of Finance whether, in view of the analysis made by his department which proves, with supporting figures contrary to the claims of the minister himself, that the Quebec proposal could help the industries outside Quebec as well in the clothing, footwear and textile industries, he will take that report into consideration and give an affirmative reply to the Quebec government, this in order to stop misleading the Canadian people by claiming that the step was taken as a separatist measure?

subsubtopic: SALES TAX-GOVERNMENT STUDY OF QUEBEC PROPOSALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have answered that question repeatedly. Over a period of three weeks, we made proposals to all the provincial governments. During my discussions with my provincial counterparts, we looked into all kinds of possibilities. We picked two out which were agreeable to the nine other provinces; unfortunately, Mr. Parizeau decided to act unilaterally after the federal government reached an agreement with the other provinces. Last Friday, through my officials, I suggested a compromise through the formula explained to the House by my colleague the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations and I intend to send Mr. Parizeau a letter if he feels the information given by his officials is not adequate.

FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT CONSULTING PROVINCES ON ENACTING NEW CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations. Given the responsibilities delegated to the minister for improved relations between the federal government and the provinces, can the minister tell the House whether he has had continued talks with the officials responsible in each province on this subject, and can he also specify if there have been talks with the officials responsible in the province of Quebec for an in-depth study of a possible redrafting of the constitution, in order to maintain harmony in our country and preserve a Canada of which we can be proud?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Laionde (Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Federal-Provincial Relations)
subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT CONSULTING PROVINCES ON ENACTING NEW CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for his question and indicate to him that I have indeed
April 21, 1978

been in contact with my provincial counterparts and even the premiers during the last few months. We have had the opportunity to discuss the matter raised by the hon. member. Unfortunately, as far as Quebec is concerned, I have not had the opportunity to discuss the constitutional question with my counterpart, for the simple and obvious reason that that government has clearly indicated through its official spokesmen, including the premier himself, that it is not interested in discussing a federal or federalist type of approach to Canadian problems, but that it merely wants separation of the country and the constitution of a country separate from the rest of Canada. Of course, the government does not endorse such an option and as far as we are concerned it is not even a negotiable option, so as long as the Quebec government maintains that position on the future of Canada and of Quebec, I fail to see on what grounds we could agree.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT CONSULTING PROVINCES ON ENACTING NEW CONSTITUTION
speechtext: My question, Mr. Speaker, was of course inspired by the statements made by the Quebec premier in Boston these past few days, where, according to newspaper reports, he stated that he has absolutely no intention of splitting up Canada. That is why I thought that the premier of Quebec and the federal minister responsible for federal-provincial relations had engaged in certain discussions. That being the case, however, is the minister willing, in light of the reply he has just given, to lend an ear to the least showing of good faith which may come from the Quebec government?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Federal-Provincial Relations)
subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT CONSULTING PROVINCES ON ENACTING NEW CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government would obviously be very happy to see a positive evolution by the Parti Quebe-cois and the Quebec government in their position, more particularly as it relates to the question of independence. Moreover, the hon. member knows very well that Premier Levesque is a master in the skilful use of words, that he has a tendency to speak with extreme moderation when he is abroad and to spit fire as soon as he is back in Quebec. Nothing in what has been said, both in Quebec and abroad, indicates any change whatever in the fundamental position of the Quebec government about the future of Canada and more particularly about that of Quebec. It is obvious that the Quebec government has in no way modified its position as far as its objectives are concerned, these objectives being its political sovereignty in Quebec and the independence of Quebec, even at the price of some economic association with the rest of Canada, the conditions of which have not yet been determined. As far as we are concerned, we believe that position is absolutely unrealistic; it is not a reasonable solution to the problems of Canada and, in our view, it is unacceptable.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege, and I am sure the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) would not deliberately misinterpret my words. When I used the term "guns" today I am sure he knows

April 21, 1978
Privilege-Mr. Stevens
what I meant. When I was talking about regulations in connection with the act which governs the new owners of long guns, guns used by farmers, ranchers, fishermen, and trappers,
I suggested the regulations had not been drafted. That act has been law for almost a year. I have looked into this matter and there are no regulations which have been approved by the provinces or the Minister of Justice. In other words, there is a law on the books without any explanation or understanding.
For example, in respect of the definition of a bona fide gun collector, we have no idea in law whether this has reference to one gun, two guns, or twenty guns. When these people apply for permits in order to get certificates they are told quite properly by the commissioner he does not have the authority to issue the certificates. If the certificates are not issued before January 1, 1978, or at least applications are received, gun collectors can never get certificates. That is what I was putting to the minister.
We have waited a whole year for this from the government, as we did in respect of regulations regarding gas and oil. These people are subject to prosecution probably because of the illegal possession of weapons of any kind, in the absence of those regulations. The minister misinterpreted my question to be related to machine guns. The Minister of Justice knows I was not talking about machine guns, but he used that answer deliberately to cover up his own procrastination.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MR. WOOLLIAMS-ANSWER GIVEN BY MINISTER OF JUSTICE DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the hon. member was not talking about machine guns, but the letter from the commissioner, from which he has quoted in this House on two occasions, is a letter relating to the registration of machine guns, in which the commissioner makes it very clear that the law states that after January 1, 1978, new collectors of machine guns cannot register what are now absolutely prohibited weapons. The law is also quite clear that bona fide collectors of weapons other than machine guns can register their guns. The RCMP is clear on what is a bona fide collector for that purpose, namely, someone whose record, on checking, does not contain some adverse comment, and nothing is known to the local registrar of firearms that would indicate the information on the application, as a collector, is false.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF CERTAIN GOLD COINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to allow the Governor in Council to authorize the Royal Canadian Mint to strike and issue gold coins, to determine their face value and specify the maximum mumber of gold coins to be struck in a year.
In 1977 the Royal Canadian Mint was authorized to issue a special 22 carat gold coin with a $100 face value to commemorate the 25th anniversary of Her Majesty. In only four months, 176,000 gold coins were sold for an amount of $24.6 million. [English]
The world annual market of numismatic coins is estimated at about $1 billion, and in 1977 the Mint sales were more than $31 million. The government believes the Mint should continue its efforts to gain for Canada a substantial share of the world market.

Such a project could yield such benefits as creation of jobs at the Royal Canadian Mint and better profitability of production services; creation of jobs outside the mint, for example for the production of related products like blanks and cases; creation of jobs in mining and related industries; and improvement of our balance of payments through the sale of coins abroad.

I trust these advantages will commend themselves to hon. members opposite and that any difficulties they may find with the bill will be resolved in a spirit of mutual co-operation at committee stage.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF CERTAIN GOLD COINS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF CERTAIN GOLD COINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I expect there will be considerable difficulties from members on this

April 21, 1978
Currency and Exchange Act
side in connection with this bill because of the possible wide powers it takes away from the House of Commons and gives to the cabinet.
This would not be the first time we have seen attempts by this government to reduce the powers of the House of Commons. I do not have to think back very far to remember the last tally we had on orders in council issued by this government. The last annual count was something like 3,300. I think we have to compare the number of orders in council used in this parliament with the number used in the British House of Commons. There, for the same period, 12 orders in council were issued, compared to over 3,000 issued by this government. It may be that through familiarity with the use of orders in council, Canadians, and even Canadian parliamentarians, have been lulled into a sense of complacence and think there is nothing wrong with this.
I ask hon. members to recall a few short years ago when we had a lengthy debate in this House on the right of the government to issue these very coins that are under consideration. The reason for that debate was obvious. Members of the opposition were quite concerned that this kind of tampering with the coinage and the money system in Canada should be taking place. I only refer to this to indicate to the House the seriousness of the measure before us.
I am sorry that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) has left the chamber. He was party to another move by this government when it attempted to remove the importance and power of this House of Commons. I am referring to an action taken within the last two months by the Minister of Justice who, while in Vancouver, called a press conference for the express purpose of announcing a matter of serious concern to British Columbians. It was a matter which should have been announced in this House, not by the Minister of Justice but by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Guay). I am referring to the matter of the importation of and duties on wide flange steel beams which are so widely used in steel fabrication in British Columbia.
The government has imposed a tariff on imported steel in order to help eastern steel producers. That move was probably understandable, Mr. Speaker, but the government had not thought it through to see how that kind of a move would affect the industry in British Columbia. It was established that the B.C. steel fabricators were not using eastern Canadian produced steel in any event. Freight rates and other factors made it non-competitive with steel that was available from overseas.
I do not mean to debate the steel issue under this bill, but I am stressing the fact that instead of the then minister of national revenue getting up in the House and saying that the government had decided to remove temporarily the tariff on imported wide flange steel, the government took that power away from the House and sent the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) to Vancouver to hold a press conference at noon Ottawa time on a Friday, which effectively closed off any
[Mr. Clarke.l
possibility of debate until Monday afternoon of the following week.
In the normal circumstances the Minister of National Revenue would have made a statement in the House. There would have been an opportunity for reply from this side and from other opposition parties, and then questions on the matter, so that it would have been fully aired. As it was, the Minister of Justice was sent to Vancouver to do it. But not only that, he had indicated in less than a frank manner after the cabinet meeting the night before that no decision had been reached on that matter. Furthermore, he indicated to the press conference in Vancouver that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) or the then minister of national revenue-I am not sure which one it was-would be making a simultaneous statement in the House of Commons. That, of course, did not happen. The only statement which was made in that case was made by the Minister of Justice in Vancouver.
Another reference which we can all remember involving the removal of powers from this House of Commons was the holding of a first minister's conference by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in Ottawa which took place down the street from this building. This conference, held during the current session of this parliament, took away from the media and from Canadians the importance of the business of this House. We can excuse the Prime Minister-I guess we can get along without him from time to time-but in this case there were more ministers than just the Prime Minister absent, which curtailed the answering of questions. As well, other members had to absent themselves from the House in order to observe the conference. I draw that to your attention, Mr. Speaker, simply as an example of attempts by the government to take away powers of this House.
Who knows at this point what the intentions are of this particular bill or what powers will be taken away from the House and given to the cabinet under this bill? What is the bill actually telling us? It allows the gold content of coins to vary. It allows the cabinet to determine the number of coins to be issued. The parliamentary secretary has set out briefly and accurately the intent of the bill. However, I would like to look at the explanatory notes to the bill, shown on page 2. With regard to clause 1 it says:
This amendment would allow the Governor in Council to authorize the issue of gold coins of different denominations and would remove the requirement that the value of the gold in the coins be equal to the amount that appears as the denomination of the coin.
What will that do to our coinage? Already under the Olympic Coin Act we have a situation where we have two categories of gold coins. In each category the gold coin has a face value of $100. We find the 14-karat gold coin contains 7.77 grams of pure gold, whereas the 22-karat gold coin contains 15.55 grams of pure gold. I do not know what reliance people can be expected to put on the value of coinage. Here are two coins both having a face value of $100 but each containing a different quantity of gold. We do not know whether it is the intention of the government to issue a Kruger rand kind of coin with a known quantity of gold, for instance one ounce.
April 21, 1978

We can refer to some other actions of the government to illustrate that the government does not let us know exactly what it has in mind. However, before I do that I want to refer to the Olympic gold coin program and in particular with regard to the advertising which was used to market the coins. A buyer was given the impression that this investment would pay handsomely within a short period of time. The advertisement states:
Seven reasons why the Canadian Olympic 22 karat Gold Proof Coin is one of the most unusual coins in history.and why you should reserve yours now!
Those words appear in large print at the top of the advertisement. Following that the seven reasons are given why these coins will increase in value. Then it opines "Yesterday's Olympic Coins are today's treasures." Then a table is given which is headed "Value of Olympic Coins-The Historic World Record". The impression created is that these coins are a good investment and will increase in value. In very small print at the bottom of the page in something like we call shyster print out in my part of the country, it says, "No assurance can be given that any particular coins will appreciate in value". It is even hard for me to read these words under the bright lights of the House here.
With that kind of advertising and the kind of content we see here, I hope that we on this side of the House can be forgiven for wondering what it is that the government has up its sleeve. I have a comment here about these particular coins:
Critics point out that the coins do not contain sufficient precious metal ($35.50 and $71 worth of pure gold respectively), to justify their face value, nor are they scarce enough to bring about large price increases.
I recognize that collectors make their own markets, and if the claims in the advertisement are correct that fewer coins are being issued than there are collectors in the world, perhaps the values will go up, although there is no assurance that the government will not be producing any more coins to take away the value contained there.
I remember a couple of years ago that the government laid a charge against an industry in this country, the particular company involved was fined, I think it was $7,000, by the courts of the land for advertising pewter beer mugs. This was a give-away kind of thing offered by one of the cereal companies, I believe it was General Foods, and these beer mugs were to be sold for $2.39 or some other very low figure. The government laid a charge against General Foods and the company was subsequently convicted, even though it would have been obvious to any person with the slightest knowledge of valuable metals that pewter beer mugs could not be sold for the price advertised. Of course, there was no pewter in those mugs at all. They were made out of some kind of metal which looked like pewter or, possibly, out of plastic. Anyway, the courts made the decision, and it is not my intention to reflect on that decision.
A similar instance occurred right here on Parliament Hill when the Secretary of State circulated a letter to all members of parliament offering supplies of desk flags, Canadian flags
Currency and Exchange Act
suitable for placing on a desk. The letter said they had a "nice gold mounting". Perhaps the expression used was "gold-plated mounting". Well, Mr. Speaker, it is not gold at all. It was merely a plastic base and a plastic stick, but they were gold coloured. I raised that point in the House because this happened about the same time the government was charging somebody else for selling pewter mugs which were not made of pewter. But neither the Secretary of State nor the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs felt that the law applied to the government. And to this day those flags are still being advertised as having gold bases and gold standards. I use this example simply to illustrate the trouble into which legislation like this can get us.
I wish to turn attention for a few moments to the history of the Royal Canadian Mint and to the circumstances in which it became what it is. It is interesting to note that for approximately the last ten years it has come under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Supply and Services. I should like to refer to the remarks of no less a personage than the Prime Minister who spoke as follows when introducing the measure to establish the Department of Supply and Services following the creation of the Royal Canadian Mint as a Crown corporation:
The most significant suggestion concerns the establishment of the Department of Supply and Services. The Glassco Commission had recommended the grouping within a single department of common services-
These are the important words-"common services"-
-such as purchasing and supply, in a way that... would be advantageous... The proposed department will be responsible for procurements as well as for other administrative services.
That will enable us to... to provide most of the common services needed by the various government departments.
Common services might very well be understood to include the issue of coinage for daily use in our commercial transactions, but I do not understand at all how common services could be considered to include the issue of gold coins or souvenir coins produced for sale or profit by the Mint.
About the same time as the Department of Supply and Services was formed, the Mint was established as a Crown corporation. It was understood that this was being done to permit more flexibility in its operations. At the present time the Mint can make a profit. This is known as seignorage. When the Mint produces certain coins and circulates them at face value, charges are made and the Mint is in a position to make a profit from their distribution. Here is a statement from the Mint itself with regard to the position:
Like any manufacturer, the Mint has problems of supply and demand and has never been able to accurately predict the requirements of the public. Under the new financing arrangements, the Mint now has greater operational flexibility and is able to adjust rapidly to fluctuating demands.
A great debate is going on at the present time as to the latitude which ought to be allowed Crown corporations. We have had experience of Crown corporations improperly using their retained earnings in revolving accounts. Moneys provided by parliament for certain purposes are subsequently used for different purposes. The Royal Canadian Mint was previously obliged to seek appropriations in parliament for each year's capital expenditure. This procedure, of course, gave the House

April 21, 1978
Currency and Exchange Act
an opportunity to examine the estimates, since each appropriation is considered by a committee. Under the new arrangements the Mint will be able to borrow funds from the treasury and build up a surplus out of its expected profits. However, the limit on the accumulation of such profits will be one million dollars-any sum in excess of that has to be turned over to the treasury. Some foresight appears to have been used there. The freedom which has been provided is, of course, exercised by the Mint's operations.
We come back to the question: what did the government have in mind when it produced this bill? I ask myself: why are we expected to relieve parliament of the task of approving the issuance of coinage? I seriously question whether this power should be taken from parliament and placed in the hands of cabinet. In my view consideration should at least be given to placing a limit on such authority by granting it only for a certain period so that we might have an opportunity to see how the new system works out. I would think a trial period of two years or so would not be unreasonable.
I trust we shall have an opportunity before parliament is dissolved to get this bill into committee and examine it in more detail, and that the government will then give us information on the basis of which we shall be able to make a reasonable decision on the matter.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF CERTAIN GOLD COINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very interested in this bill. I do not know why it has been presented in this way. It leaves a lot of decisions up to the cabinet, and ministers may find themselves facing the same questions as the Post Office does in relation to the issue of stamps.
The government has now found out something which I knew a long time ago; it is that we have never really gone off the gold standard. We have played around with it. We have fooled around with substitutes. But when the crunch comes, gold is important because of the respect paid to it by people all over the world, not only for its value in terms of coinage but for its worth as a precious metal to be hoarded or saved.
The value of our dollar has risen slightly in the last day or two, not because the minister is spending hundreds of millions of dollars to bolster it but simply because the United States says it will take gold out of Fort Knox and put it on the market to bolster the American currency. Our currency is the tail on the American dog. The value of our money went up a little because the issuance of gold from Fort Knox to the international market to buy American dollars resulted in a stronger American dollar.
In the sixties I asked the then minister of finance to consider establishing a gold coin for the centennial year, 1967. There were three ministers of finance after that before one would agree that a gold coin should be issued for our centennial. That had not been done for many years. The minister of finance I First spoke to was a Conservative, Donald Fleming, and he would have nothing to do with that because he had decided that the American dollar was all-powerful and that he did not

want to put a price on gold in Canada. The only assistance Canada was giving to its gold industry was in providing emergency gold mines assistance.
After much discussion with three ministers of finance it was decided that Canada would put out a $50.00 gold piece for our centennial year. I do not know how much one of those would be worth now, but 1 wish I had a hundred of them. They would be worth more than bonds, speculative oil stock or anything else, because their value went up tremendously. They were so good that when the 1976 Olympics were in such great difficulty it was agreed to put out another gold coin. However, there was so much confusion that some people were unable to get a series. Some people were able to get only one out of the series. This caused great difficulty for collectors. The indication was that we could not over-produce because there was a large market for gold coins.
The government must have learned, although that is not indicated in this bill, that once it decides to mint a coin which is to be used mainly by collectors, it has to go on the futures market. I am very unhappy that the government will not say how much gold is in the coin and that it will not be redeemable for that amount of gold. Our history of gold coins indicates that gold coins have never been common tender.
Gold coins are not seen on the market. They are not seen crossing bank counters. They are not used for tender because their intrinsic value as collector's items is considerably higher than their face value, even if that face value fluctuates according to the market, and there has been considerable fluctuation at a reasonably high level.
If we decide now to put out gold coins, we should indicate the reason, what use will be made of them, and how many will be issued. If we can stabilize gold in Canada by developing the Kruger rand system or some other system, we will solve much of the problem of our falling dollar and certainly much of the unemployment problem in my area because there are literally dozens of gold mines which could be reopened. They have very high employment factors because of the type of mining involved. Many of these mines could reopen if a stabilization of the price, to eliminate some of the fluctuations, were guaranteed. I doubt if we will mine very much more gold in Canada unless there is a big incentive. We will not produce much more than we can use for our own currency.
I am pleased that we are going ahead with this operation, but I am surprised that we are leaving it up to the cabinet. This is a beautiful way of bootlegging. How many hon. members have received complaints because people could not buy nickel dollars last year?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF CERTAIN GOLD COINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before lunch I mentioned that I welcomed this bill and the decision on the part of the government to make gold coinage a regular part of the operations of the Mint. Also I mentioned the difficulties we were facing in relation to acquiring gold coinage at the present time. Obviously something has gone wrong with the Mint, because it is very difficult for my constituents and for other coin collectors to get coins from either the Mint or their local banks. Yet they see coin dealers selling fairly large amounts of coins. For example, the current issue of the silver dollar is sold by coin dealers at anywhere from 25 cents to 75 cents higher than the cost of purchase from the banks or the Mint. Obviously the coin dealers have some edge on that market, and a great deal of bootlegging apparently is taking place.
We are interested in the production of gold coins other than as legal tender. I agree that they have to be put out as legal tender in order that they will qualify in the field of numismatics. What is happening in respect of this currency is that the coins are all being retained by those individuals who purchase them as a security investment or for some some other reason. In any event, they are being kept off the currency market.
There are other gold currencies being traded in Canada. It is possible to go to the bank and buy gold coins manufactured
Currency and Exchange Act
in England, and Kruger rands are quoted on the Canadian exchange, as well as several other gold currencies.
These coins contain a certain amount of gold, but they are not traded for the face value but for the value of the gold content on world markets. As a result this value fluctuates from day to day. I presume this will not be the case in respect of the currency we will be producing and it will not qualify under the Currency and Exchange Act. We were not talking about currency with a face value of less than $2, including one and five cent pieces, or perhaps other coins of a value less than $10. What we have in mind are coins that will be considerably more valuable than this, such as gold coins of $100, $200, and $500 denominations.
For these reasons I think these coins must have an established mineral content and a specified value in order to serve the purpose I want served, that is, these coins should provide the Canadian producer of gold with an outlet, with a value that is fair and reasonable to those purchasing the coins, rather than making the coins specifically for the numismatic industry. That market is a world-wide market and, as the parliamentary secretary has suggested, it amounts to something in the neighbourhood of $1 billion a year. A great proportion of the gold coins manufactured for that purpose would find their way to that market. I want to see more involved than just that. These coins should be produced in a form that will be purchased by the people because they have a known value. Coins produced for numismatic purposes do not necessarily fall into that category.
Our present act states that a gold coin has to contain a certain amount of gold equal in value to at least the coin's face value. That is to be changed. That is not a big change, as we have done it with everything else. Up until 1968 our silver coins contained silver. Following that we switched to purely nickel coinage. I am surprised that people are still buying silver dollars and fifty cent pieces which contain no silver at all. As far as the fifty cent pieces are concerned, it is difficult to find any, even though they contain no silver at all. Our commonly circulated coin contains no silver, but it has a value as legal tender. I am wondering why there are so few of these coins available. The minister or his parliamentary secretary should give an explanation to parliament about what happens to this coinage. We mint a very large number of silver dollars each year, although they now are nickel dollars, and we mint a large number of fifty cent pieces, but to my knowledge no bank in Ottawa had any fifty cent pieces this year. They were all absorbed by the numismatic industry.
What we are talking about is the feeding of that industry and the bootleg market in coins. I do not know whether the Master of the Mint is getting rich, but he damned well should be. You will remember that there were investigations on a couple of occasions about things that go on, some of which would lift your scalp, I suppose. Somebody is doing very well in respect of our coinage. The silver and gold industries are not doing very well at the moment in Canada. If we are going to get into this business we should be willing to share some of the

April 21, 1978
Currency and Exchange Act
profits with those industries, thereby putting people back to work in those areas of high unemployment.
I have no objection to the governor in council making the decisions regarding the denomination of the coins and when they should be minted, but I do not think we want to add just another $100 coin to our production. These coins should have some significance.
This whole thing may be likened to our postage stamps. We must be supporting almost every artist in the country as we are putting out more stamps than it would be possible for you to buy, and certainly more than a young stamp collector could afford. I buy stamps, although I am not sure why as I am not a collector. I have bought corners for years and just left them in my office. The last time I looked they had disappeared. I am not really much of a collector, but I do buy them. Considering the number of notices one receives of new stamps coming out, one would have to pay $5 or $6 on occasion just to buy a new issue. These stamps are becoming very high priced and we are turning them out like they were going out of style and we were going out of business. I have no real objection to that, but I would like to see some less expensive stamps. With the prices we are paying for them now we must be getting them done by Goya, and I have in mind that series put out a little while ago with ships and things.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF CERTAIN GOLD COINS
speechtext: It wasn't this Goyer.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF CERTAIN GOLD COINS
speechtext:
No, I am sure it is not this Goyer, but some famous artist. In any event, these stamps are very good, and we can be proud to have them travelling around the world. I have in mind particularly a fourteen cent stamp put out recently.
In any event, I think the same should be true of our coins. Part of the intrinsic value of our coins is in how they look. We should give credit where credit is due. The Mint has done a beautiful job with these coins. Perhaps it has not done any better than Franklin or probably one or two other private mints around the country, but for some reason the coins minted in Canada are beautiful.
It is interesting to note that a number of countries throughout the world have their coins minted in Canada because we do such a nice job. I suppose our Mint will do the same with these gold coins. The responsibility will not be that of some committee. The minister must assume some responsibility in this regard, and I would not like to see the same old game played. I have seen this happen at least two or three times in respect of postage stamps.
A decision must be made as to what denominations are to be put out and how many of each coin will be minted. Then much of the business can be given to our mining industry in Canada. I suppose it does not matter a damn which way we go, but let us at least buy what we need for these coins from the industry in Canada. The last time we bought silver and gold for coinage we did not buy nearly enough. The first half was at a very low price, and when we went into the market the second time to buy enough to finish the run we were paying almost twice as much. So, if there is any money to be made from the advan-

tage that our coinage will have on the market, surely some of it should go to the mines themselves, and we should buy it in a pre-set block. There is nothing unusual about that.
Ontario Hydro has done that very thing with the mining industry. They have set a block aside and said that they will buy that over a period of time at a set price. Therefore, they know how much it is going to be. It is less than wise for the Mint not to have their full run either ahead of them or the price set in the futures market so that they are not involved in that speculation that takes place once a decision is made to make a new coin. I commend the government for finally having made the decision that to mint gold type coins in Canada does not mean that we are back on the gold standard. I am not prepared to argue whether or not it would be good to go back on the gold standard.
As I mentioned earlier today, when the Americans decide to take money out of Fort Knox in the form of gold and put it on the market, it is going to help our dollar, and we are quite a piece away from Fort Knox. It will certainly help their dollar as well, so maybe it is a relationship that we should honour. Certainly, in relation to the hoarding of coins through collections and in other manners, we are going to have a ready market for these gold coins provided we do not overdo it by manufacturing too many at a time.
If a gold coin is used for tender, it should be such that it is evaluated on its gold value as well as on its face value. There should be some relationship. This is not possible in a free market; therefore it was probably necessary to take that out. There was really no point in changing the section that said that you could use gold to make your full transaction or full tender. Now, under the proposed bill, only one coin can be used towards that tender each day in transactions. If it is going to be called a tender, then it should be available to make the total payment, and I do not think that it should be restricted to this one coin.
I welcome the decision, Mr. Speaker, and I hope that this means that in co-operation with the mining industry we can provide a stable base price by our future orders, and that that stable price will allow many of the gold mines throughout very distressed parts of Canada-northern Ontario, northern Quebec, northern Manitoba-to reopen so that work can take place in those mines for the advantage of communities that were built on them. These communities have always been subject to the fluctuations that are influenced very greatly by decisions of government, and I hope that this is one decision that will be favourable to them.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF CERTAIN GOLD COINS
speechtext:
This little two-clause bill, Mr. Speaker, would appear to many to be a very innocuous bill, but I would suggest that it is in fact the contrary. This bill seeks to eliminate for the government the problems it had over the debate when Olympic coins were set off. That debate did not have the proper arguments, and it was a bad case.
April 21, 1978

I am sure there are some people who would confess right now-and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) is one of them-that they shared a lot of doubts about the Olympic gold coin issue. Oh yes, one remembers! Now, however, the ministry of which he is a part seeks to give power to the governor in council to act on its own without getting parliamentary sanction. There are those purists who will say, "Oh, but the House committee for statutory instruments would have a go and could comment upon it." This is not the case. This is not like the Post Office. In the Post Office case, which is now of current debate, it is a question of whether there is legal power to so act to pass the order in council. Under this bill there will not be a question of legal power to issue gold coins of a partial value, debased value, or a glittering value, because the power will be there. The governor in council is to be given power to issue coins of various rates, that is, to use the language of the bill:
-of the denominations and standards of fineness specified in Part I of the schedule ...
Automatically there will not be any more such controversy. I do not know why they are asking for that. This is a point the parliamentary secretary failed to explain to the satisfaction of the House, and is also a point the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) will have to explain when he comes to committee.
It is interesting to note that C-39 in the Revised Statues is the number, in those statutes, of the Currency and Exchange Act, a pure coincidence. There was a debate last year with regard to part of this act because certain amendments were brought in whereby with respect to the foreign exchange fund, which is audited by the Auditor General, there is no longer a requirement that the audit report be made to parliament but that it be made to the Minister of Finance. The minister then has five months after the end of the year, as I recall, to submit the report on the status of the foreign exchange fund during the previous year. I believe the House was divided on that point, but this particular matter deals with two areas. The first area is determining when the governor in council can issue gold coins.
As the act now stands, and I am wondering why the act was not amended to make it conform to present circumstances, the conditions that apply in C-39 Revised Statutes, have not been eliminated entirely. Apparently under the old act, as was established another act of parliament and as is being maintained, Canada is on a floating dollar. Therefore, there is no value to the dollar on the basis of gold value, so this is eliminated.
The wording of section 4(1) of the Currency and Exchange Act will be as follows:
The governor in council may by proclamation authorize the issue of gold coins-
The old section 4 is being subdivided into three subsections. The first subsection continues as follows:
-having the description, standards, remedy allowance and least current weight specified in Part 1 of the schedule.
Currency and Exchange Act
Then the governor in council is given authority to issue other new gold coins, not those specified in the act but coins of an undisclosed nature.
Subsection (2) reads as follows:
The governor in council may by proclamation amend Part 1 of the schedule by adding denominations of gold coins other than those specified therein and prescribing ...
In other words, as the governor in council sees fit, so shall it act. This House will have no recourse whatsoever not even through a review of the order in council because the order in council shall only be reviewed as to its legality, not as to its intrinsic value.
Subsection (3) reads as follows:
The governor in council may by order specify the maximum number of gold coins of any denomination specified in Part 1 of the schedule to be struck in any year.
We need an explanation of why these changes are being made, and I can advise the parliamentary secretary that these explanations will have to be forthcoming. There can be no pressure put on opposition members on the committee because of a pending election. At this late date it is pointless. There has been plenty of time to get bills through, and there will be competition for time in the House for measures arising out of the budget which are important.
The second point is that the bill changes the status of coins in so far as their being legal tender is concerned. Hitherto legal tender consisted of gold coins for their face value, because that was the value of gold. We know now that value is around $160 or $165 per ounce, and no gold coin can contain gold to that value because the size would be too big. We are going into a debased gold coinage and it is going to ruin the market, unless you get one with the figure of a nude dancing girl on the back that is struck upside down, or with some other peculiarity that will make it of extraordinary market value.
We also want to know why it will not be possible to pay any account with more than $10 in 25-cent pieces for $1 coins. Ten dollars is the maximum legal tender on any one occasion. There is nothing to say that I cannot walk into a store where I owe an account and put down the $10 payment in pennies, however, and then go out and return with another $10 worth of pennies.

We are playing around with coins here, Mr. Speaker. I wonder why a limit was placed on the legal tender of coins. I can see no particular reason for it. A reason will have to be offered by the Minister of Supply and Services or whoever is acting on his behalf.
Those are the two purposes of this bill, Mr. Speaker. I am rather surprised that we have not heard any comments from backbenchers on the government side, although an explanation was offered in part. I am not too sure the parliamentary secretary understood what she was telling us, and 1 am sure some of her cabinet colleagues did not understand it either, unless they had the translator on.
Why is there a rush to bring this bill forward at this time, to be followed by Bill C-36 which requires a great deal more examination than this one? This bill is to go to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates, which is a strange venue for it. It should really go to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. Is the reason to leave that latter committee free to deal with Bill C-36? The finance committee has before it the finance estimates and the industry, trade and commerce estimates, so Bill C-36 will have to take its place.
Ministers will be sounding the alarm on several bills because of a pending election and claiming that they must have the legislation. Mr. Speaker, this House does not take cognizance, officially, of a pending election. It has the responsibility to examine estimates until May 31. They have first priority. I think it is an abuse of his position for any minister to come along with legislation now. It points up the nonsense of the committee structure. These are the people who instituted that form of committee where the same committee is charged with the study of estimates and legislation. The Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs is usually the butt of most this pressure. Ministers do not appear, or find that they have other things to do.
I want to interject my views on a matter that was raised earlier on a point of privilege, after question period today. This matter was in regard to the duties of a minister to appear before a committee examining his estimates. It was suggested in the past that action should be taken by the procedural committee to provide some sort of sanction, some sort of rule, compelling the minister to appear on his estimates. All I can say is that a minister who does not appear before a House committee with regard to his estimates is failing to discharge his duties. He is misplacing his priorities, and he is actually giving affront to the House. He is responsible to the House. However, all too often cabinet ministers suddenly become statesmen. It is their scale of priorities that suddenly becomes the most important.
I will refer to the scheme of committee structure which I proposed through the procedure committee along with my colleague, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro), and other members on the other side of the House who agreed with my proposal. Some who felt that they had

greater knowledge of the rules and the practices of this House objected to my form of committee structure, but no one has been able to come up with anything that begins to match the flexibility of the system which was proposed. We would not be faced at this time with the difficulty, I suggest, which may face certain government ministers, if the committees of the House had the backbone to stand by their duty to examine estimates with which they are charged, and for which they have so little time to carry out.
Now, a minister merely has to appear only as frequently as is decent, leaving the rest to his officials. For any sessions for which he is being closely questioned, with a ten-minute question period, the minister can consume the questioner's ten minutes with eight minutes of inconsequential answers. He only has to go through about 90 minutes a session. It is the old business of "just keep a low profile, duck your head, or pull in your head like a turtle and ride it out". That is how much control the House has on a minister with regard to estimates. It is nonsense. I would like to hear one minister from the government side defend the present structure-one of them.
In so far as these bills are concerned we do not know when this House will end. These bills will go to particular committees. We will see some other legislation possibly on Monday. Tuesday is an allotted day. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) has given notice to us of the coming forward of a bill to implement his customs tariff proposals in the budget. They stay in the House in committee of the whole. All of this will take more than next week. Therefore, to say sittings of the House must necessarily come to an end next week is nonsense. It is nonsense, because there are certain ministers here who will ask for legislation to come forward and who will be most insincere. I do not agree that there should be this pressure.
On miscellaneous estimates I certainly intend to ask my full share of questions of the Minister of Supply and Services when, and if, he gets around to us on this particular bill. We certainly intend to go into any other bill that comes before the committees, as they should. I do not intend, because there is a pending election, to neglect the discharge of my duties, nor do my colleagues. I expect the same from the conscientious committee members on the other side of the House, and there are some who will do a good job. They will have to be satisfied as to the validity of these legislative proposals.
It may be that we will reach Bill C-36 this afternoon. Because that bill is not so simple a bill, there are a lot of questions which the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is going to be asked. With these few points I am quite prepared to see this bill go to the Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates to see what explanations we can get. I reserve my position depending upon those explanations.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF CERTAIN GOLD COINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it had not been my intention to speak to this bill. However, as I sat here and listened to some of the comments being made, my curiosity was aroused and I read the bill carefully. I wonder what we are getting into. I did not hear all of the statements being made. I followed the introductory comments made by the parliamentary secretary. As I said, my focus of attention
April 21, 1978

was not on the bill at that time and I do not know whether an explanation, in the absence of the minister, was given. It does seem strange that the minister should be absent when a bill in which he is interested is before the House. I should have thought that this is one of the prime roles of a minister, to introduce and to shepherd through the House, at least in the introductory days, a bill in which he has some concern.
There remains this question in our minds as to why a minister is absent when a bill standing in his name is brought before the House. It is not just an ordinary bill but a bill with royal recommendation. There are funds involved, and the minister has assigned his parliamentary secretary to introduce this bill.
Then we come to the timing of the bill. This has already been referred to by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). These days were considered at one time to be the days when we were winding down and it might be thought that these bills of secondary importance, perhaps, are being introduced to fill in the time? Are they being used to fill in the time? Are we under pressure? Are we being pressured? This raises a question in my mind too. I have a feeling we are being put under false pressure in order to get some of these bills through. There seems to be some disinclination now, for one reason or another, for better or for worse, to wind down this tension that has built up over the last couple of weeks and put off that evil day, an evil day for the government. But it will be a great day for the country when that election comes, I can assure you.
We have been subjected in this parliament by this government to a reign of error. Unbelievable, a reign of error! This government has committed one error after another. That is what we are confronted with. We are being asked to put through a bill of doubtful priority, so much priority that the minister is not here. I have my curiosity aroused on the second point.
The third point that grasped my attention was not curiosity. It was fear, because of the provisions of the first clause. I think it is worth reading into the record. Those who read Hansard do not always know the terms of the bills we are considering. The first of the amendments we are being asked to approve reads like this:
The governor in council may by proclamation authorize the issue of gold coins having the description, standards, remedy allowance and least current weight specified in Part I of the schedule.
I notice that even in the development of this bill and its presentation to the House of commons, possibly by oversight on the part of the public service which put it together for the minister, they did not even bother to include schedule I as it stands. It is not being amended. The idea is that this parliament shall have no further opportunity to amend this schedule.
I went to the library while my friend was speaking to get a copy of schedule I. I looked at it. Then I looked at the second part we are being asked to amend, 4(2), having in mind "may
Currency and Exchange Act
by proclamation authorize the issue of gold coins" under part I. The second part reads this way:
The governor in council may by proclamation amend Part I of the schedule by adding denominations of gold coins other than those specified therein and prescribing the description, standards, remedy allowance and least current weight for each coin so added or specified therein.
What's cooking? Why should we be asked to allow the governor in council to proclaim the issuance of coins under this schedule in the existing act and then be prepared to grant to a government like this the authority to add and change, not just the number of coins, but the standards, the amount of the standard weight, the number of grains in each coin, the standard millesimal fineness of each coin and the remedy allowance.
I am not sure, but I suspect the remedy allowance is the degree of variance from the standards, plus or minus .5 grains or, in the case of fineness, plus or minus 1.5 millimeters. I suppose that is what it is. Also, the least current weight can be changed.
There is a footnote in part I of the schedule which indicates that the least current weight of 280.59 grains means that when a coin has through usage, through the passage of hands-and I am not sure gold coins will pass through that many hands- been worn down to the point where it no longer weighs more than 280.59 grains, it must be withdrawn from service. Thereupon it could be melted and reduced or added to another coin.
The whole operation of granting a government power by proclamation to issue gold coins is fair enough. It is probably within the purview of a government. However, to authorize any government, this government in particular, to change the denominations, standards, remedy allowance and least current weight is something at which I balk. If this government had a better record of performance in any area, I might have been prepared to consider agreeing. I cannot grant this government the right to debase the coinage. It could reduce the amount of weight contained in the coinage. That is what they want this authority for. However, why do they want that? My curiosity is again titillated. I cannot make out why they are aiming in this direction. I think the right expression is to strike coinage.

-in French, la monnaie est frappee, is it not? I believe the translation in English-

Recently a new medal was struck and sent to Canadians. Each member of this House was sent a copy of the Silver Jubilee medal honouring the occasion of this twenty-fifth year of Her Majesty's reign. Good. Fine. Excellent. The medals are good. They are well designed.

That goes for the large medal, but do you think you can find a miniature? Do you think it is possible to find one in this town? They just do not make them here. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) has been talking about how he has been forcing Canadian industry to do this and that. However, they do not even make miniatures in this country. Why does the Mint not make them?
For three weeks I have been trying to get a miniature so that I might wear it proudly when I am invited to a formal occasion, whether it be at Rideau Hall or the Lieutenant Governor's in British Columbia. In fact there are people in high places in this country who have asked me whether I can get a miniature for them.
Do you know what is happening? The suppliers of these medals are sending to Britain asking that the miniatures be sent to them so that they can be sold here. However, it is the British Silver Jubilee medal not the Canadian one.
The Queen's head on both medals is identical, but the reverse side of the Canadian medal is a distinctively Canadian design, and so it should be. I have no objection to that. In fact I am proud of that. It is a good design. However, you cannot get the Canadian design in this country. Why has the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce in collaboration with his friend, the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer), who is primarily responsible for the conduct of the Mint, not worked out a scheme whereby the miniatures would be struck by the Mint and made available to the Canadian people? I asked about this in a committee earlier this week.
I understand this medal was issued to some 7,000 members of the Canadian armed forces. I am delighted. I am sure they have earned them and will wear them proudly. I am glad it has been extended to them and to a number of other Canadians.
There are 7,000 miniatures that might have been part of the commerce of this country from our Mint. Never a thought was given to the idea that they might be struck by the Mint. Why not? I am at a loss to understand how that opportunity might have been lost by our Mint which has done such outstanding work both in the minting of Canadian coins and coins abroad.
When I was serving abroad, I had some of these suppliers of metals come to me in Costa Rica to ask if I could introduce them to people at the central bank. They wanted to take orders for supplying the metal for striking in Canada of the coinage of these foreign countries. This is good business, yet the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is not applying for this business. He is not paying attention to it at all. The Minister of Supply and Services is not paying attention to it either. Yet they say they are interested in developing Canadian industry.
On the four grounds I have mentioned I shall find it extremely difficult to support this bill. As we all know, it is impossible to amend a bill at this stage; we just have to outline some of our ideas and misgivings. I suppose it could be defeated on second reading, but I doubt it. We have all asked numbers of questions to which answers will be required in

committee. I am sure the Minister of Supply and Services could have been here. He is not presiding over a group of international bankers.
Incidentally, I might remind hon. members that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) was not singled out at the meeting in Vancouver for election to the Chairmanship of the assembly there. It is simply a matter of international courtesy that the minister of finance of the host country is chosen chairman. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) told us the hon. gentleman was out in Vancouver and made a point of adding that he had been elected chairman. Well, he was elected chairman because he was minister of finance of the host country. One feature which disturbs me is the absence of the Minister of Finance.
Then again, the timing of the bill gives rise to some uncertainty in my mind. Further, it would be parliamentary suicide to accept the second clause; we have been asked on far too many occasions to agree to parliament withdrawing from whatever it is doing and allow the government to take over. Not this government, thank you.
Also, I wanted to draw the attention of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to his failure to get the Mint involved in a profitable business, that of striking miniatures and selling them. It looks as though the hon. gentleman will not be proud to wear his Silver Jubilee medal. That is for him to decide. I think we should have commissioned the Mint to strike those medals and make them available to Canadians. I will have a lot of questions to ask when this measure gets to committee.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF CERTAIN GOLD COINS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I came into the House in the middle of the speech of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich and I intend to emphasize the cogent arguments he advanced. I see the cabinet is strongly represented here today; of that multitude of 33 ministers there are four present in the chamber. That is par for the government course when there is a bill before the House.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF CERTAIN GOLD COINS
speechtext: We don't see you here often on Friday.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF CERTAIN GOLD COINS
speechtext:
We are not the government but we shall be soon, and we would not be trailing all over the country when we should be here. To my mind this is complete contempt of parliament, another example of the government making a eunuch out of this institution. I have every regard for the hon. lady who is the parliamentary secretary, but we are being asked to deal with a gold bill, a bill changing the law with respect to the content of certain coins, and no responsible minister is here. I do not think we would have got much further if the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) had been here. I understand that the uselessness of the Minister of Supply and Services has been well established by now. I understand he is about to be translated to the repose of a high government executive position based upon trade and the expansion of trade in this country.
When I think of him I often think of him as the $20 million kid. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, the situation in which those
April 21, 1978

dollars disappeared and we never got an explanation of what happened. The Minister of Supply and Services is concerned with the subject under consideration today. He should be here to explain, though I do not think he would be able to explain in any case. When I see parliament treated in this way I am reminded of the words of Cromwell to the Long Parliament: "In the name of God, go; go at once." I would only add, to bring those words up to date: "Go, Goyer, go without any possible delay". It is making an abomination of this institution.
This must be an important bill. It is one which has to be passed before the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) ultimately reaches the conclusion that he must go to the country. He has fooled around for the last ten days or so trying to find some explanation for the apparent change across the country. One of the hon. members over there shakes his head in the negative.
This bill has to do with gold, but there was another recent incident dealing with Goldfarb. Goldfarb operates some kind of poll. He is close to the government. My information is that in the last few days he has produced a prophecy which indicates that all is not well for the Liberals in Toronto and in Ontario. So the Prime Minister is not here today. He is away.
Oh, since I started to speak I have added 20 per cent to the number of ministers in the chamber which indicates the attractiveness of my contribution. What is the purpose of this bill? Why the rush? I followed my hon. friend from Victoria who asked why the right should be given to the governor in council to add denominations of gold coins other than those specified therein and prescribe the description, standards, remedy allowance and least current weight for each coin so added. What is the purpose of this? Is it the intention to issue an emaciated, depreciated currency? Is the government not satisfied with the present standard of gold coins? Does this proposal for turning over the power to the governor in council to determine the gold content of each and every coin indicate that there is a desire on the part of the government to get this bill through for a purpose as yet unknown and in respect of which no information has been given? This is just part and parcel of the course that is being followed.
We sit, we ask, we endeavour to get information and we hear from the government that it believes in freedom of information. Fifteen hundred questions which would have been embarrassing to the government, many of which have been on the order paper for the last six, seven or eight months, are still not answered; and when this parliament ends those questions will not be answered. That is the contempt which is being shown to parliament. Never have I seen anything like this. I remember the days of war under the Right Hon. Mackenzie King when secrecy was necessary in many cases in the interests of the protection and preservation of the security of the nation. But we were able to get information. We cannot get it today. The government says it will not answer.
I do not condemn the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) in any way. He has been condemned for the budget he introduced the other day. He had no more to do with that than I had. The
Currency and Exchange Act
determinant was the Prime Minister, following the course that he has in finance of determining what shall and shall not be brought in.
That is the reason the Hon. John Turner and the hon. Donald Macdonald are no longer here. They would not dance to the Prime Minister's tune. However, parliament is now asked to do that. If there is anybody in the group of ministers which is here, including my hon. friend the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), ''than whom there is no whomer," to use a western expression, I would like him now to rise and tell the House exactly-and I know he has the information-what is the reason for this. Is this going to improve the trade of Canada? Is this going to advance the cause of those who believe in the necessity of an expansion of trade for this nation?
What is the reason that parliament is being asked by order in council to allow the government to depreciate Canadian gold currency? That is all I want to know, and there may be a perfect answer, at least one-and we will not look at the political consequences-which, if it comes from the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, I feel sure would be most revealing. I do not want to hold him up. I want to give him the opportunity of letting the House know what nobody else among the ministers present knows.
The Minister of Supply and Services is hightailing across Canada at our expense. The Prime Minister is in Toronto for the purpose of finding out whether Goldfarb knows what he is talking about in his prophecy that all is not well for the government. We want to know, not about Goldfarb, but why the gold standard of this country should be depreciated with the opportunity given to the government to do it by order in council. This is a step which has never been taken before. This is a step which ought not to be taken now.
I am going to sit down, knowing how this government has trodden on the rights of parliament and turned this institution into a place where we simply talk and debate. The government does not listen and relies on its majority, regardless of what arguments are advanced. What is the reason for this? Why has the government suddenly decided here on a Friday afternoon, with ministers all over creation, to bring in this piece of legislation which cannot but have the effect of adding still more knowledge in the Canadian people and people all over the world internationally that Canada's dollar is falling and falling, and that, today we are in a position where Canada is not in economic difficulty but actually in a depression and even worse than that?
I recall very well that when I was prime minister we valued the dollar after the president of the United States decided to try to destroy the Canadian government. We valued it and set it up, finally, at 92.5 cents. What did the Liberals say? I am speaking about the Liberals then because they are not that today. They are the Trudeau party today and since he has taken over. They said, "Oh, this is terrible". That 92.5 cent dollar brought the greatest trade Canada has ever had internationally, and I was glad to hear the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce the other day-and he is now applaud-

April 21, 1978
Currency and Exchange Act
ing exactly what I am saying because he has not forgotten those days-say that the only thing wrong with the present value of the Canadian dollar was that apparently it should even be lower.

speechtext: He wants a zero dollar.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF CERTAIN GOLD COINS
speechtext:
I am very happy to see a reformation in the thinking of the hon. gentleman so far advanced among those members of the cabinet with whom he now sits, and I am waiting with bated breath to see him rise and hear him say, "Yes, I know the Diefenbaker government was right when it fixed the rate at 92.5 cents".
The minister just applauded that statement on my part, but those who today sit around him said, "We will do away with it as soon as we come into office". They waited six and a half long years before doing it. The greatest trade this country ever had was during that period following the fixing of the value of the Canadian dollar. However, we did it by act of parliament, and whatever the change by order in council in the gold standard in so far as the content of gold coins is concerned, I am against it. It is dangerous. It is apparently some trick which has been worked out which can only have the effect internationally of Canada's credit going down more and more week by week.
Today, as a result of the actions of this government and the deficit of $10 billion, Canadian taxpayers are paying $5.6 million a day in interest on the amount of the deficit which had to be borrowed. Let us hear from one of these responsible ministers of the government. One minister has left. He knows nothing more about this than he does about his own department, so I do not mind his absence. I greatly admired the courage of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce a few moments ago when he approved what my government did, because those with whom he sits now kept it for six and a half years.
I now ask him to get up and with the clarity which is naturally that of any westerner clear the situation. The Prime Minister is not here. He is finding out how bad conditions are in Toronto and elsewhere. I ask the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to rise now and let us know what benefit will come from an order in council procedure being set up to enable this government to depreciate Canadian gold coins.

It would increase the direct liabilities in the corporate accounts to $10 billion, the contingency liabilities of
April 21, 1978

the Export Development Corporation would be increased to $10 billion, the direct liabilities in the government accounts to $2.5 billion and the contingency liabilities to $3.5 billion.
The Export Development Corporation has done a tremendous job in assisting Canadian exports by finding and creating markets for Canadian produce. subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce

This is an essential piece of legislation. The hon. member is asking if we ever get any back. Actually a profit is made, and it does quite well creating jobs in Canada.
The right hon. member for Prince Albert referred to trade. Canadian exporters are winning business abroad on the basis of quality, price and delivery. The purpose of the Export Development Corporation financing is to match the officially supported financial competition from abroad. EDC is experiencing an increased level of business. It must remain in a strong competitive position in order to support Canadian exports. By the end of this year, the corporation will have lent out something in the neighbourhood of $2 billion. Obviously with expanded trade there is a need for expanded financial assistance and contingency liabilities.
Also the right hon. member spoke about the exchange value of the Canadian dollar with respect to currencies as well and major national competition. Certainly the present situation is a great boon to export trade and manufactured goods. Last year there was a $3 billion surplus in exported goods and I believe it will be higher than that this year.

Export Development Act
