speechtext: The previous bill which was sent to committee will create jobs, as well as a market for Canadian gold. When the right hon. member for Prince Albert was prime minister, there was an act before parliament entitled the "Gold Subvention Act" under which gold mines were subsidized. subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I am attempting to speak on the legislation which is before the House now. It has to do with enlarging the liabilities and the contingency fund of the Export Development Corporation. It is a very important piece of legislation and I am pleased that it is before parliament today. I hope it can be sent to committee quickly in order for the Export Development Corporation to come before the committee and answer all questions that the right hon. member or anyone else would like to put.
The ceiling on corporate loans is $4.25 billion at the present time. That ceiling will be reached by the middle of June. Thus, it is important to deal with this piece of legislation now. If the bill is not passed, it will mean a loss of new jobs and could occasion many lay-offs. It would result in a tremendous loss in Canadian exports, and it would not assist the economic recovery which would take place if parliament did not pass this piece of legislation before the summer recess.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: What about an election, Jack?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
An election would be fine with me, but it is not my prerogative.
The Export Development Corporation is probably the most misunderstood corporation in Canada. Many members of the opposition, as well as many people across the country, do not really understand what the government and the EDC are doing. Some months ago lay-offs occurred at Inco. A great deal of concern was expressed because Inco had constructed

April 21, 1978
Export Development Act nickel mines in Guatemala and Indonesia, and it was said that somehow or other jobs were being taken away from Canadians. In that particular case, the Export Development Corporation provided approximately $20.75 million for the mine in Guatemala and $57.25 million for the financing of the mine in Indonesia.
Let me explain what really happened. The project was going ahead and Inco came to the Export Development Corporation and wanted some insurance on the financing. They said they would procure about $1 million worth of goods in Canada. The Export Development Corporation said that $1 million worth was not nearly enough, and, by negotiations, increased the expenditure for manufactured goods in Canada up to as high as $60 million.
In the total project involving the building of those nickel mines in those two countries something like $900 million was spent, financed by Japan, Germany and Great Britain, and the Export Development Corporation helped to sell the mining equipment to those mines in both of those countries. The mining equipment we sold really involved something like 4,800 man-years of employment in Canada, so the Export Development Corporation is creating jobs.
Another very good example of the work done by the Export Development Corporation in creating jobs in Canada can be found in the announcement on April 5, 1978 of the biggest insurance agreement yet supporting $1 billion worth of sales by Bell Canada to Saudi Arabia with $250 million in security insurance and $180 million in export credit insurance. This contract will provide at least 2,500 man-years of employment for Canadians.
I am just picking out a few specific projects to give parliament and the Canadian people some idea of what the Export Development Corporation really does.
On March 9, 1978 loans totalling $57 million supporting engineering and mining equipment sales valued at $67 million by the Canadian firms of Sandwell and Company Limited of Vancouver and SNC-Rust Limited of Montreal to Argentina were made. Here again a tremendous number of jobs were created in Canada. This money does not leave Canada but goes to pay for the procurement of the Canadian manufactured machinery used in these projects.
During a visit to Mexico the chairman of the Export Development Corporation, Mr. MacDonald, offered lines of credit totalling $1.45 billion to help foster Canadian trade to that country. Mexico is deeply interested in developing its oil and gas industry. We have the expertise and believe we can sell the machinery needed for oil production and mining, and for that matter for pulp and paper, power generating plants and urban transportation projects, all of which are being eyed by Canadian firms for sales to Mexico.
In January of 1978 Alcan International Limited was awarded a $30.6 million contract for the construction of an alumina plant on Aughinish Island, Ireland, with the support of an Export Development Corporation loan.

In December of 1977 four loan agreements were announced involving $50 million for the sale of five electrical generators to Venezuela by Canadian General Electric in Scarborough; a $3.75 million loan to support a sale of $4.4 million by Cana-dair Limited of Montreal for two CL-215 water bombers to Greece; and a loan of $5.5 million to Romania supporting sales of $6.9 million in pulp and paper plant equipment by Combustion Engineering-Superheater Limited of Ottawa. The fourth loan amounting to $1.45 million was in support of a sale of $1.7 million by Douglas Aircraft of Malton to Finnair Oy for wing, floor and tail assemblies for DC-9 aircraft.
The Export Development Corporation on December 20, 1977 extended a $285 million financing protocol to Poland and announced a $46.1 million loan supporting a $52.1 million sale of capital goods and equipment to that country by thirteen Canadian exporters for the Kwidzyn pulp and paper mill in that country. These are loans made for the procurement of Canadian equipment to assist those countries in their own development. If we had not got into the business of guaranteeing or insuring the loans, some other country would and we would not be selling pulp and paper mill equipment, aircraft, mining equipment and the other things I have listed.
On a per capita basis, exports represent $2,000 per person in Canada; and as a percentage of our gross national product, exports represent about 22 per cent. Canada is one of the most reliant on exports of any country in the world. In 1976 it ranked seventh among the largest world trading nations in terms of value of exports and second in terms of exports per capita.
This gives the House some idea of how important exports are, and of the continuing role that the Export Development Corporation must play in order to assist this country in meeting and creating job needs, and attaining the world trade potential that is at our feet.
We must look increasingly to the export of goods and related services for economic growth and to strengthen the industrial sector. Many times I have heard members in the House say our manufacturing industries cannot compete, or that we have too large a deficit in manufactured end products. Certainly the Export Development Corporation has assisted tremendously in increasing our exports of manufactured goods.
It is imperative that this piece of legislation be passed because it means so much to the creation maintenance of jobs. Last year alone it is estimated that the work being done for export under financing or insurance by the Export Development Corporation created or maintained something in the neighbourhood of 200,000 jobs in Canada. Many times we hear opposition members talking about unemployment and the need for job creation. I can say to you, Mr. Speaker, without worrying about recrimination, that I have been negotiating with the opposition to get speedy passage on second reading in order that the bill can be sent to the committee where hon. members can examine the operations of the Export Development Corporation. Questions can be asked and answers can be given quickly so that the bill can come back to the House and pass, as it is needed before the end of June. If there is an
April 21, 1978

election, as hon. members have been suggesting, we may not have the chance of passing this legislation until the fall. This would seriously hurt Canada's export trade.
There are 50 principal Canadian exporters and 220 subsuppliers involved in 42 agreements in 22 countries. Three loans totalling $95 million were made on behalf of the Government of Canada. This gives some idea of the scope of this corporation. It is not just a small thing but involves a great many companies. In fact, it is used extensively for almost all our trading off the North American continent and used as well quite extensively in trading with the United States.
This will give some idea of the importance of this tool which Canadian exporters have learned to use in trading particularly with that group I might refer to as third world countries who want to buy manufactured goods. Canadian firms today are bidding on $5.5 billion in goods to be sold in the Middle East. We have acquired in the Middle East to date approximately $1.2 billion of trade and bidding on another $5.5 billion. All of these sales are managed through the Export Development Corporation through either insurance or guaranteed loans.
I do not intend to speak any longer, Mr. Speaker, but I do urge that members give speedy passage to this bill. It will be referred to the finance committee, and the Export Development Corporation is very anxious indeed to come before the committee and explain how important it is to our export trade and over-all picture, particularly to manufactured goods which everyone will agree create a great deal of employment in our country.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to put a question to the minister to clarify something in his policy. While I was listening to his address on this bill, I was looking at a news release put out by the government which is dated October 14, 1976. It reads:
The Export Development Corporation (EDC) will lend up to $102 million to finance the $113 million sale of Canadian equipment for a world scale integrated pulp and paper complex near Kwidzyn, Poland.
The Kwidzyn project consists of a bleached Kraft pulp mill with a capacity of 150,000 metric tons per year-a semi-chemical pulp mill of 50,000 tons per year capacity and a paper mill with an annual output of 270,000 metric tons. Also included in the project are recovery units, steam generators, water supply and effluent treatment systems.
Such a project will undoubtedly provide a lot of jobs in Canada.
I also know from my studies of the east coast fisheries problem that if we in Atlantic Canada under the present circumstances are to catch and market squid, capelin, silver hake and argentines-to name four species of soft fish which must be frozen immediately when taken from the sea-we require freezer trawlers of a minimum length of 230 to 240 feet. Our studies and pricing techniques have told us that these trawlers have been built and provided by Poland at a cost some 25 per cent lower than we can build them in Canada.
My question to the minister is: How is it that we can loan money to Poland for the construction of paper mills, or that
Export Development Act
they are willing to buy this equipment in Canada at a price which must obviously be 25 per cent higher than it would cost to build it in their own country, when we in turn must, if we can get the government to move on the construction of freezer trawlers, build them in Canada at a 25 per cent higher cost? subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF AGE OF COMPULSORY RETIREMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my understanding that this is the second time we have had the privilege of debating the motion of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), although it is the first opportunity that I have had to become involved directly. I am delighted to be able to take part in the debate on this topic, which I see has had a lot of consideration from many different quarters all across this continent and perhaps even around the world.
First of all, I notice that the other place had occasion to debate a very similar motion on six different days. The latest date of debate in the other place was December 7. On conclusion of the debate on date, the motion was agreed to. That motion referred to a special committee the subject matter, being mandatory retirement at the age of 65. The special committee of the other place was to examine and report upon the existing retirement age policies affecting workers in both
4764

April 21, 1978
Age of Retirement
the public and private sectors; the social and economic implications of mandatory retirement based on age alone. I do not think I need to run over the details completely of the motion of the other place but suffice to say that consideration was given on six occasions and the subject matter of the motion was referred to this special committee.
That is not the only place where consideration has been given to this subject. I would refer the House to the congressional record of the United States Senate where less than a month ago, on March 23, a motion to put an end to mandatory retirement was considered and the vote was taken on that date. The result was yeas, 62 and nays, 10.
They have an interesting practice in that chamber, Mr. Speaker; they indicate the number of members not voting on that day. The number was 28. A further interesting wrinkle in their procedure is to announce how absent members would have voted if they had been present. Accordingly, Senator Stevens is reported as saying: "I announce Senator so and so". He then lists about eight of the absent senators, stating that they were necessarily absent and that if they had been present and voting, they would have voted yea.
Those are a couple of high-powered considerations of this motion. It would be my hope, at the end of the debate on this motion today, that this House might also approve the motion of my colleague the hon. member for Edmonton West. It asks the government to consider the advisability of enacting legislative proposals to raise the compulsory retirement age from 65 to 70 for any person aged 65 or over who does not wish to retire and is prepared to give up any entitlements to any private pension plan or annuity.
I want to refer to some other considerations of this problem. It is a serious problem and it has many implications. It is not just a simple matter of whether or not a person wants to work after the age of 65. There are such considerations as whether a person over the age of 65 continuing to work deprives some younger person of a job. There is also the effect of forced retirement on an individual who is forced to retire in the midst of a productive life.
There is a further complication which could be helped by the passage of this motion. I refer to the so-called age bulge that we have in Canada today. If we continue on the working cycle that we are presently embarked upon, there will be a small number of workers by the end of this century to support the very large number of retired people. The statistics go something like this: Presently we have seven workers for every retired person. It is expected that that number will be reduced to three workers for every retired person by the end of the century. The effects of that are obvious. The tax burden on those three workers will be more than double what it is today in order to provide for the support of the individuals who are then retired. By passing this motion and the following legislation, we could alleviate the very serious problem which will be with us by the late 1980's and certainly by the end of the century.
I want to refer again to action in the United States Congress. Consideration has been given in that legislature to that

matter. Writing in the Congressional Digest there is this foreword to an article headed: "Revision of Mandatory Retirement Age Policy". It starts out:
Pending in the 95th Congress is legislation which, if adopted, could have major impact on the work habits and job opportunities of millions of older Americans. Already passed by the House of Representatives and near floor action in the Senate in somewhat different form are proposed amendments to the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA) which would bar mandatory retirement for any worker under age 70 who wished to continue in his job and who was able to do so.
The measure, which would not prevent retirement at an earlier age, is directed at those persons in the American work force-in private industry as well as State and local government-who now are forced to retire at a specified age, most commonly 65. Civilian employees of the Federal Government are already subject to a mandatory retirement age of 70, the level which pending legislation would establish for all covered workers.
The date of this issue is November, 1977. The motion reached the floor of the United States Senate last month. I imagine we can all point to examples of cases where people continued to carry out useful occupations past the age of 65. We have some notable examples of that in this House. The retirement age for members of the other place and members of the judiciary in Canada today is 75 years. I know of many workers doing far more active work than what is entailed in being a Senator or a judge, such as those cleaning and doing other manual work. Many thousands of Canadians involved in voluntary work are well beyond the age of 65 or even 75.
The history of this kind of legislation goes back a long way. I have an article here which mentions legislation pushed through in Germany by von Bismarck, First Chancellor of the German Empire in 1889. That legislation allowed their older citizens to continue to work and raised the need to define old age. In Great Britain similar legislation was passed in 1908 using the age of 70, later reducing it to 65.
I have many pages of references to the desirability of this kind of legislation to permit older people to continue to lead useful lives. I have explained the advantages I see to the economy and the employment situation as a whole. I do not think any great purpose would be served by making further reference to the body of information that I have here. All the evidence that I have been able to lay my hands on supports the view. It is my feeling that, given the opportunity, this House would also support the view. If there are any contrary views, I suggest they be given to us now so that those who wish to contribute to the debate will have an opportunity for rebuttal.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Kenneth Robinson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF AGE OF COMPULSORY RETIREMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) for bringing this matter before the House. He first brought it before the House on November 7, 1977, suggesting that there be an extension of the age of compulsory retirement. I would like to read his motion again:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of enacting legislative proposals to raise the compulsory retirement age from 65 to 70 for any person aged 65 or more who does not so wish to retire and is prepared to give up his/her entitlements to any private pension plan or annuity.
April 21, 1978

This motion is most timely indeed. We are all pleased to have the opportunity to speak on this motion today.
The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) pointed out that the whole question of aging has become a consideration in Canada. He stated that in the next decade, and without doubt before the end of the century, there will be greater numbers of senior citizens than ever before as a percentage of our population. He pointed out that members of the other place and of the judiciary retire at the age of 75. I note there is no age of retirement in the House of Commons. I think that is rather significant.
In making this motion, the hon. member for Edmonton West is dealing with a subject, namely retirement, which has tremendous potential implications, touching as it does on financial, economic, social and health issues, not to mention political considerations. Certainly this is a current topic which has been receiving growing coverage in the press and has been a focus of attention for governments both here and abroad.
But the subject of retirement is also one of baffling complexity which does not really lend itself to simple solutions. I am sure that in making his proposal, the hon. member for Edmonton West was less intent on revising retirement ages than he was on making all members aware of the problems facing society, both now and in the future, in this important area. Indeed, in earlier debate on this motion the hon. member indicated his awareness that there is no compulsory retirement age in Canada at present. This fact has a distinct bearing on this debate, since it reflects a certain freedom of choice and adaptability to conditions which would be difficult to achieve with an over-all mandatory retirement age.
Perhaps we should examine for a moment some of the issues which are involved in any discussion on the subject of retirement. In the light of these issues, we can then, if time permits, look at a few of the proposals which have recently been made, including the hon. member's suggestion, and place them in perspective.
One of the most obvious and important factors determining an individual's decision to retire is the state of his or her health. I am sure every member of this House has experienced days when, no matter how exciting the prospect of the day's work was, it was difficult to work up enthusiasm for the tasks at hand because physically, for one reason or another, we just did not feel up to it. Most of us are fortunate enough to spend most of our lives in good health, but not all are so lucky. It is an unavoidable fact that, as our bodies age, they become more susceptible to problems. Bones become brittle, break more easily and take longer to mend. Resistance to many diseases and complications such as pneumonia is lower. Perhaps some day, with dramatic medical advances, the situation will change. However, for most Canadians declining physical strength is an inevitable function of the aging process.
True, for some-and we need only look about the House for examples-this process moves more slowly. Unfortunately, for others, whether as a result of accident, disease or genetic factors, aging is accelerated-I believe the expression used is "premature aging".
Age of Retirement
It used to be that for many Canadians retirement from the labour force was a physical necessity. They simply could not work any longer. They could not cope with the physical and mental demands being made upon them day after day. Much of the rationale for the development of pension or retirement systems was to enable people to retire by ensuring that they had the financial resources to leave the work force. Pensions were an innovative move to help such people.
Today, of course, many people who retire are not physically or mentally hampered significantly from pursuing a career. Studies tend to support the observation that most early retirees-that is, men and women who leave the work force before the retirement age normally associated with their particular work of profession-still do so primarily for health reasons. This is a vital consideration to bear in mind before making any move to raise retirement ages.
Those who must leave the work force earlier because of their health should not find their financial situation inadvertently adversely affected. To counterbalance this possibility, many who advocate the pushing ahead of retirement years simultaneously propound the necessity for more comprehensive disability plans and suggest this avenue of assistance for those who find themselves unable to continue working.
Concern has been expressed for those faced with not only the measurable effects of physical deterioration but also the special difficulties imposed by the pressures of change, technological and social. It is unquestionably an over-generalization to say that you cannot teach an old dog new tricks. The fact of the matter remains, however, that many people as they grow older are not as flexible in their ways, ideas or approaches. In many areas of endeavour this rigidity is a definite liability both to the employee and the employer. Those who defend compulsory retirement at age 65 or earlier often point to this problem, and underline the humiliation to an employee who must be told he is incompetent, rather than that he has simply reached the normal retirement age.
Of course, the financial aspect of retirement is equally important. The costs are something that too few Canadians really consider in advance. A person who retires can rarely count on an income after retirement which compares at all favourably with his income from work. Income from government sources such as the Canada Pension Plan and old age security provides a secure base of income which is adequate to meet basic needs.
But what about the additional income the individual undoubtedly desires? This must come from private savings or a company pension. The latter, even where it does exist, will usually only replace a significant portion of pre-retirement income for an employee with a record of long service for the same employer. Also, private retirement savings are something to be encouraged. All members, I am sure, have welcomed the additional flexibility for registered retirement savings plans recently announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chreti-

April 21, 1978
Age of Retirement
en). But personal savings of this type requires a good deal of advance planning.
Timing is clearly critical. A person who plans to retire at age 60 is going to have to start building up adequate income sources over a relatively short working career to provide for a longer retirement period than a 65-year-old would have. Conversely, someone who works to 70 years of age, as under this proposal, would have a relatively shorter period of retirement to plan for, on average, and a longer time to build up secure income sources for retirement.
The financial cost to the employer must also be remembered. An employer willing to provide for employees retiring at 60 or 65 will have to put more money into a pension plan than he would if employees generally were staying on until age 70. On the other hand, the employer will have to pay the wages of these senior employees, and many times will feel that a younger worker would be more productive at less cost.
This leads us into the economic aspects of retirement. All too little is known of the potential economic effects that a change in retirement ages could have. The age of workers in the labour force could affect levels of employment, the size of the work force and the general productivity. Purchasing patterns and savings rates would obviously be different if people were generally planning for retirement at 70 as opposed to 65 or 60. The economic burden on the working population which the retired population represents would also change dramatically. This ratio of retired to working Canadians will change over time in any case, and this is something that has caused concern for many experts.
The effect on employment opportunities bears some study, since it is one of the most controversial aspects of the whole retirement issue. Proposals for raising the retirement age are opposed by some on the grounds that they are taking opportunities for employment from the unemployed and denying advancement to younger workers. Countries like Denmark have instituted strong inducements to early retirement for such reasons. I hope to touch on their policies at greater length a bit later.
On the other hand, there are those who say that we should not just raise the retirement age, but abolish retirement altogether. There is no doubt that retirement is one of the most traumatic of life's experiences for the retired individual and his or her family. Many prove unable to cope with this situation, especially in a society based on the work ethic and oriented around the work experience.
Much of the problem is clearly a matter of planning on the part of the individual and society as a whole. Most people, it appears, still do not give retirement any serious thought until immediately before they get their gold watch, if then. Preparation for retirement in educational, psychological, financial and social terms should be undertaken by the individual. But this is changing, and increasing numbers of employers offer preretirement sessions in the same way as they offer training or orientation sessions for new employees. Community colleges and non-profit organizations are coming into the field as well. The scope and quality of the programs offered is improving

and will continue to improve as more experience is gained and more feed-back received.
It is interesting to note that, when surveyed, the preferences and perceptions of persons five or ten years from retirement differed noticeably from those of persons already retired. This has been especially true of the particular topic with which we are dealing today-the age of retirement. It reflects an actual difference in attitude, but perhaps it is also a result of the experience of the retired person as opposed to the less realistic viewpoint of the person who has not yet experienced departure from the labour force.
Certainly, knowledge of and preparation for retirement are important. Another approach is to change the nature of retirement. The idea of gradual retirement-taking on less strenuous or demanding work; working shorter hours; having longer vacations; working into a second career where interest rather than income is the principal impetus-has been proposed, examined and tried at various times by various people. What we seem to be finding is that there is no single solution for everyone.
In this light we can examine some of the proposals which have been made concerning the retirement age both here and elsewhere. It is of interest to note that different countries have proposed different solutions to the various issues I have outlined. While the United States appears to be moving to extend the mandatory retirement age to 70, many European countries seem to be moving or already have moved towards earlier retirement. In Italy, where retirement is currently at age 60 for men and 55 for women, labour unions are striving to reduce the retirement age for men to 55. In France, employees in private firms who opt for retirement at age 60 rather than 65 are paid 70 per cent of their last salary until age 65, when their normal pension comes into effect. Companies employing these workers are expected to replace them with workers under 25. However, few appear to be taking advantage of this offer.
A somewhat similar program exists in Belgium which, I understand, requires employers to replace those opting for early retirement with unemployed people under 30 years of age. Belgium also prohibits pensioners from gainful employment, as do Finland and Ireland.
In Denmark, the government is proposing to pay an "after wage". Workers over 60 but under the national pensionable age of 67 will qualify for this voluntary retirement payment if they have contributed to an officially recognized unemployment insurance scheme for five years or more. The so-called "after wage" offered is only 90 per cent of the current maximum unemployment benefit offered in Denmark, but such unemployment benefits may rise as high as $15,000 per year. It is apparently the hope of the Danish government that such a program will generate new job openings for they young. However, it is my understanding that many in that country feel jobs vacated by older people will not be made available to the young but merely create an opportunity for employers to reduce their work force.
April 21, 1978

In the United States an entirely different approach to the retirement problem appears to be developing. Recent legislation passed by Congress and signed into law by President Carter on April 6 of this year raises the mandatory retirement age in the United States to 70 from age 65. The law will become effective in September 30 of this year for all federal government employees and effective January 1, 1979 for all other workers in the United States. The bill allows those between 65 and 70 to continue working as long as they meet a competency test. Senator Pepper, the 77-year-old Florida Democrat who sponsored the bill, now apparently wants to go even further and abolish age entirely as a criterion for mandatory retirement.
I hope I have made clear, Mr. Speaker, that at present there are conflicting points of view regarding the issues concerning retirement, and different governments have taken different approaches to solving these issues. This confusion of ideas and solutions may lead us to question whether the time is ripe for fundamental changes in the Canadian retirement system such as would be implied by the hon. member's proposal.
At present, as all members here are aware, the Canada Pension Plan and the Old Age Security Act are neutral regarding retirement age. Benefits are available at age 65, but beneficiaries are not required to be retired. It is true that many private employers in Canada have made age 65 the mandatory retirement age. Many others, however, have developed pension plans containing provisions which explicitly permit the deferment of an employee's retirement date. Thus, there is considerable flexibility already available in Canada and many Canadians are taking advantage of this flexible system.
To quote figures previously given, in September of 1977 there were some 188,000 persons over age 65 still in the labour force, of whom 64,000 were over 70. At the same time, there were many others who have entered retirement before age 65, for a variety of reasons. Nevertheless, this issue of retirement is one which must always be borne in mind, and I thank the hon. member for his efforts in bringing it to the attention of this House.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF AGE OF COMPULSORY RETIREMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to participate in this debate. Despite what the hon. member suggests in his motion, there are still many Canadians who work beyond age 65 and, in so doing, make a valuable contribution to our economy and our society.
Nevertheless, while we may not agree that the initiatives proposed by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) are necessarily the most appropriate for achieving the goal which he seeks to achieve, it is refreshing to hear some concerns being expressed for those Canadians who believe that their productive years are not necessarily over when they reach some arbitrary age such as age 65.
This is a considerably different approach from that taken by a number of persons who in the past have pressed not for the postponement of retirement for those who wish to continue in
Age of Retirement
the labour force but, rather, for lowering the eligible age for a whole range of benefits such as old age security and under the Canada Pension Plan. Some have even proposed the imposition of a mandatory national retirement age of 65 or 60 years of age in order to thrust bodily out of the labour force our country's most experienced and skilled labour.
It is rather interesting to consider what reasons we might have for taking such steps. Why do people want to retire at age 65? The use of that figure as a pensionable age is commonly attributed to Bismarck, who actually set the minimum age for retirement at age 70. That occurred more than 100 years ago. Because of the low life expectancy at that time Bismarck apparently felt that a retirement age of 70 would ensure that very few people would live to collect any pension from the state. This is assuredly not the case at present. The majority of Canadians today live to collect their old age pensions for a considerable length of time.
The idea of retirement at age 65 has taken hold rather more slowly in this country than in others. Old age security benefits, for instance, became payable at age 65 only in 1970, and the Canada Pension Plan retirement benefit has been available at age 65 without retirement and earnings test only since 1975. I might note that Sweden, which is often held up as an example for social security, lowered its retirement age from 67 to 65 only in 1976.
Regardless of its origins, however, we do at the present time have 65 as a fairly constant retirement age throughout the world. It may have become normal because it is the age at which people become entitled to retirement benefits under the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan. But I emphasize that there is no federal legislation making retirement mandatory at that age or at any other age.
Even where employees are offered earlier retirement there are usually not very many takers. I understand that since the public service has had retirement available at age 55 with 30 years' service, the average retirement age has dropped by only a year and is still well over 60. Yet we continue to hear the suggestion that the Government of Canada should consider dropping the retirement age for old age security and Canada Pension Plan purposes from 65 to 60 or even make retirement mandatory at that age. It seems we are in love with round numbers. Very few people have suggested a retirement age of 62, 63 or 61. They seem to want to take things five years at a time.
There is nothing magic about 60 as a number. I suspect that if we adopted that figure and the whole country followed suit, we would then find somebody suggesting that the age be reduced to 55 or some other number or perhaps have some other radical individuals suggesting that 50 would be even more appropriate. Clearly, the retirement age of 65 is not engraved in stone, but is there reason to believe that it is too high a retirement age? I do not know. Perhaps it is too low.
Since life expectancies and average health in our population seem to be on the rise, should we perhaps not be thinking in terms of going even beyond the suggestion of the hon. member for Edmonton West in encouraging people to remain in the

Age of Retirement
labour force? If some sudden break-through in medical science raised the average life expectancy by 20 years overnight, I am sure most people in this country would wish to reconsider their plans regarding retirement age. Yet the interesting point is that average life expectancy has risen by more than 20 years in this century. Perhaps it is legitimate to ask whether Canadians wish to have this reflected only in the lengthening of the portion of their lives which is devoted to the pleasures of retirement, pleasures which are not unalloyed, as many older Canadians would quickly advise.
The idea of raising the retirement age, which is what is suggested by the hon. member, is not idle speculation. In 1933 retirement at age 65 was made compulsory in the public service of Canada in an effort to reduce staff during a time of severe austerity. Ten years later this country was at war and that order had to be suspended. In fact, all over this country thousands of retired people went back to work and proved quite capable of doing a job and doing it well. We are told that the world wars did much to change our views on the role which women should play in our social and economic life. Perhaps we should have learned the same lesson about the elderly and retirement.
A somewhat similar phenomenon might be occurring now. Much of the pressure to lower the retirement age in Canada stems from the belief that by retiring people early we will be making room for the hiring of unemployed and young people who are currently entering the labour market in great numbers. Unfortunately, there is really no reason to assume that retiring the old will make way for the hiring of the young. Employers will not find in an 18-year-old the skill and experience which is lost when a 60-year-old employee retires. Sometimes, also, employers may take the opportunity to automate jobs out of existence.
However, we can look a bit farther down the road and see that a change is taking place in our population which will cause this pressure for early retirement to slacken. I think this is very important. The present flood of young people on job markets is a result of the so-called baby boom which occurred after the second world war. It is no secret that this boom is long since over and that the birth rate has plummeted. Zero population growth is no longer a goal to be achieved; it is a fact which exists in Canada today. It is a goal which has been surpassed, at least in the sense that we can foresee our population beginning to decline because of the lower birth rate.
This means very simply that the surge of workers entering the job market will also begin to decline in years to come. We are told that in less than a generation from now it is more than possible that this country will have a negative unemployment rate and not a positive one. Yet in terms of what we are discussing this afternoon, if we accept the principle espoused by many Canadians, we will have the people with the most skill and experience leaving their jobs at earlier and earlier ages.
It seems quite possible that the pressures which now exist will be reversed in the future and more and more people will be

suggesting 70 as the normal retirement age, as the hon. member has. In fact, as the population ages and the percentage of the population in the over 65 group continues to rise, it may be less of a suggestion and more of a necessity to keep people at work later in life. Such a prospect might cause far less dismay among the elderly than we suspect. I am sure other hon. members would find it interesting to know how many retired people would really have preferred to work for several more years before retiring. We might find that many would have preferred never to retire. I wonder if it would be possible to find out through Statistics Canada or some other agency how many Canadians were forced to retire from the private sector and how many actually retired by their own choice and not by that of their employers.
I wonder if we should address ourselves to questions such as: are there sufficient leisure time activities to ensure that Canadians will find a long period of retirement to be a satisfying and fulfilling experience? I am reminded of a story which was told to me by a chap. It dealt with what we were doing in the age of technology, the fact that we can fly from Paris to New York in four hours. It used to take eight hours four or five years ago, and much longer in the years before that. Then the question arises: what is the point of saving four hours if there is no reason for being there at an earlier time? What in fact has been saved?
Perhaps a similar situation arises when dealing with retirement and whether it is satisfying and fulfilling. I am sure for many people their greatest satisfaction and fulfilment lies in their work. Traditionally we do not expect artists, statesmen or politicians to stop working at the age of 65. No one asked A. Y. Jackson to hang up his paint brush at age 65. What type of world would we be living in today, if Winston Churchill had been forced to retire at age 65 in 1939? What would this House be like if members such as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) had taken advantage of retirement at age 60?
I feel the entire approach toward retirement in this country could benefit from a more flexible attitude. As we practise it in Canada at present, retirement is one of the most sudden and wrenching physical, financial and emotional dislocations which people undergo in their entire lifetimes. The stress of a sudden switch from regular work activity to inactivity has been known to cause premature aging and even death in people who might have had many years of a healthy and productive life if they had continued working in their occupations. This phenomenon is so common that doctors have referred to it as the "retirement disease".
There are numerous alternatives to an abrupt and final withdrawal at any age from the labour market. For example, some older individuals might prefer to keep working at productive activities but with shorter working hours, longer weekends or longer vacations. Others might wish to keep working but move to a job which would be less demanding physically but
April 21, 1978

still productive. Some countries have introduced systems whereby a person over a given age can obtain a portion of the regular old age pension while continuing to work on a parttime basis. Therefore, to a large extent we applaud the motives of the hon. member for Edmonton West for moving this motion.
Even after retirement there should be activities-and not necessarily leisure activities-in which older Canadians can participate. The success of the New Horizons program is ample evidence of the useful part senior citizens can play if given the opportunity. Unfortunately we tend to think of senior citizens as a population of helpless individuals who require monetary support in ever-increasing amounts at even earlier ages, rather than as an untapped source of creativity, energy and productivity which would help improve the quality of life for all Canadians.
I would be remiss if I did not conclude my remarks by referring to a phenomenon which occurred in the last several years. Basically people can set their own retirement age by investing in registered retirement savings plans, which reduce their income tax loads during their highest years of income. In fact, there is a mechanism which guarantees a secure future regardless of their employer and many other factors. Perhaps this is something which should be looked at very closely. As most of them are set up at the present time, either a lump sum is paid at age 65 or it is in the form of an annuity at that same age. However, perhaps it would be in the interests of both the companies which provide this service and Canadians to have a more flexible retirement savings plan. The plan could be open-ended, so that an individual at age 55 or 58 could start his program because of illness or for some other reason. The age could be at his own choosing, realizing that if he does not wait until age 65, the amount of money he will receive will be proportionately less. It would be less because it is calculated on an actuarial table as to how long an individual will live beyond the age of 65.
In conclusion, there are many alternatives to retirement at age 65. Because of health, some people may wish to retire before that age. Government and private programs should have the flexibility to meet that need. The individual who works beyond the age of 65 for his own very good reasons also should have the benefit of this flexibility so that he can continue a productive and full life, if that is his desire. God help us if government and other agencies are somehow given the power to make all the decisions affecting our lives.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF AGE OF COMPULSORY RETIREMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, certainly one can appreciate the reasons for which this motion was made. Currently a number of people are suggesting that retirement activities require a good, hard look.
I thank the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) for making this important topic the subject of the debate before the House at this time. While I agree with his motion in many ways, personally I take exception to his placing a definite cap or figure on the retirement age. Compulsory retirement should not be introduced at any age. A person is
Age of Retirement
best suited to make up his own mind physically, mentally and in every other way as to when and if he should retire from the work force.
Perhaps I am borrowing from the hon. member himself, but if I can play the role of the devil's advocate this afternoon I should like to refer to some of the contrary points of view which have been expressed. I mean some of the proposals to make retirement compulsory at even earlier ages and the various reasons for them. I should like to bring to the attention of hon. members the arguments which have been advanced by those in favour of compulsory retirement ages. Certainly I would not suggest that all the arguments are valid, but they must be put on the record and discussed. It would be useful to delineate those views in order to clarify the implications of the motion of the hon. member.
It has been suggested that the retirement of older workers is essential in order to open up opportunities for younger employees to gain advancement and make a contribution to progress by bringing new ideas and attitudes into the work force. Undoubtedly there are different outlooks, on the part of individuals in their late sixties and those in their late forties, regarding corporate and social life. I notice there are some younger people present in the gallery this afternoon. Many of them indicate that they want an opportunity which is now being held by a senior member of a corporate firm or by a senior planner in a plant. Perhaps that senior employee is reaching age 60 or age 65, and if that man retires, vacancies will be opened up all the way down the line. Thus, younger employees will be able to move up more quickly and achieve the goals which they have set for themselves in their working careers.
However, I might add that all of us who are here probably thought the same way when we started in the work force, whether it was in teaching, in a profession as a doctor or a lawyer, or whatever our profession might have been. We have looked around and seen those who had served that profession or that field of endeavour well and had attained some degree of recognition, and with that degree of recognition had attained some degree of age as well. We tended to make a comparison between the fact that they perhaps might have been grey of beard or head, in some instances without hair whatsoever, and the conclusion that it was simply because they had reached a certain age and a certain stage in their development. We soon learned, once we had gone through the work force or the profession we had chosen for ourselves, that it is not advancing years that give you progress through that business or profession; it is through the attainment of knowledge and skills and a good amount of very hard work that these people reach the positions they hold and for which they are respected.
Our attitudes change as we go along in our lives from the time we are thirty, to forty, to fifty and so on. I think that really cannot be looked upon as a serious suggestion for

April 21, 1978
Age of Retirement
bringing our retirement age down to a lower level, or even putting a cap on it, by any stretch of the imagination.
As the hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Robinson) said, somebody has said that you cannot teach an old dog new tricks. That may be true, but I can assure him that the old dog can certainly add a lot of smart wrinkles to the tricks he has already learned, and in so doing make the job he has easier for himself and for those who may follow. I do not think you have to teach an old dog new tricks; he can teach you something on the way through.
It must also be admitted that some workers will not be as capable of withstanding the rigours of employment at an advanced age as some others. This may be more obvious in physically demanding pursuits such as mining, forestry and farm labour, to some extent, though I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, there are farmers in my area who are exceptionally capable at the age of seventy, and some even beyond that.
If I might impart one small incident that happened recently in my area, let me state there was a lady in one small community who was slated to celebrate her 102nd birthday. It was a real event for the community. On the morning of the event there was quite a stir raised in the community because a number of people had tried to reach her on the telephone and could not get an answer. Of course, what immediately came to mind was that something had happened to this dear, sweet lady, and she was unable to answer the telephone. A convoy of cars took off and went to her house to see what had happened. They found out what had happened. This lady, knowing it was her 102nd birthday, was concerned that people would visit her house and find it not up to scratch. She was up on top of a twenty-foot ladder cleaning windows! That gives the House some indication of the physical capabilities of some of our senior citizens.
However, this applies as well to the white collar worker, to some extent, who perhaps cannot respond as flexibly to the pressures that can occur at critical times in almost any type of work environment. In some cases it is felt that employees lose the ambition and drive necessary to carry out their tasks, especially at more senior levels of industry. In such cases a mandatory retirement age avoids confrontation and possibly humiliation to the older worker by being demoted or worked around or even fired for incompetence after what may have been a distinguished career with faithful and competent service and work. If we take a very close look at the statistics, we will see that this has not proven to be the case.
It is the experience, knowledge and ability gained by that worker over the twenty, twenty-five or in some cases even thirty years he or she has spent in a particular field of endeavour that gives the competence that cannot be matched without that length of service and without that devotion, and in some cases, as has been said, without the blood, sweat, toil and tears that have gone into it.
Thus a mandatory retirement age has been said to maintain an upward mobility, avoid embarrassing decisions for the employer and allow the employee gracefully to withdraw from the labour force. We must always be reminded of what is lost when these years and years of experience and training come out of that labour force or particular profession.
Many have argued that compulsory retirement at an early age would also help to ease the unemployment situation among the younger workers of the labour force. It is pointed out, for example, that unemployment is highest among the very youngest workers. It is argued that by retiring the older workers, positions would be freed for younger persons to fill. I think I should say here that this is a rather unsatisfactory argument since such a move would only serve to redistribute unemployment rather than create any new employment.
I must also, if I may, make one personal observation here. This type of attitude tends to put into focus the growing attitude of some young people in our work force today, or of some people who are entering the work force today, that the only way they can be successful is by starting where their fathers left off. To me this is a rather sad commentary to be made, to some extent, because I believe the young men and women we have coming into our work force today do have the ability to start where their fathers started, from scratch, with the ability to show the devotion, aptitude and determination their fathers and our fathers showed before us in a career or a job. If there is any move to take away that urge from young people coming into industry or labour, it certainly should be looked upon as a serious thing for the people and the country.
It is also claimed that many employers would face critical financial problems if they were forced to keep on older employees who are in receipt of higher salaries as compared to less senior workers. It is true that pension costs might decrease in some cases since the employee could not draw a pension while still actively at work. However, it would be anticipated that health, disability and group life insurance premiums would certainly spiral upwards; thus a compulsory retirement age might have a disastrous effect on the cost of these pensions and medical benefits that are taken into the planning of the work force and industry today.
